claims.text: Authentic Chinese dishes and tare here typically use wheat-based soy sauce; no wheat-free soy sauce is indicated.

This is an okonomiyaki, teppanyaki, and kushiage (battered fried skewers) restaurant. Okonomiyaki batter is wheat-flour based, kushiage skewers are breaded and deep-fried, and dishes such as yakiudon are wheat-based. Everything is cooked on a shared teppan griddle and in shared fryer oil, so gluten cross-contamination should be assumed. This is not a celiac-safe environment, and no gluten-free accommodation is documented.

Okonomiyaki sauce and soy sauce are central to the cooking here, and most Japanese soy sauce and okonomiyaki/yakisoba-style sauces contain wheat. Assume these contain wheat unless staff confirm otherwise.

No vegan options are documented. The menu centers on eggs, meat, and seafood (negiyaki with eggs, meat and beef skewers, fried udon), and everything shares a griddle used for animal products. There is no indication of plant-based accommodation.

This is a coffee shop whose signature items are fruit sandwiches and egg sandwiches made on wheat bread, plus baked goods. There is no advertised gluten-free menu and no verified GF accommodation, so it is not celiac-safe. A diner with celiac disease should avoid the bread and baked items and confirm any other order directly with staff.

The menu centers on dairy (fresh cream, milk-based coffee drinks) and egg sandwiches, so vegan options are not advertised; vegan diners should ask staff what, if anything, can be prepared without animal products.

This is not a celiac-safe restaurant. The core menu is built on wheat: chuka soba and ramen, udon, soba, and breaded/fried items like tonkatsu and fried fish. With shared pots, broths, and fryer in a small everyday diner, cross-contamination with gluten is effectively unavoidable.
Documented signature dishes are wheat-based ramen and udon in soy-sauce broths, with no indication of any gluten-free preparation or separate cooking surfaces.

The broths and seasonings are soy-sauce based (the chuka soba is a chicken-and-soy-sauce broth). Standard Japanese soy sauce and dashi typically contain wheat, so the soups and sauces here should be assumed to contain gluten.

Not suitable for vegans. The kitchen centers on chicken-based broths, pork (chashu), egg dishes, and dashi, all prepared in shared equipment; there is no indicated vegan option and high risk of animal-product cross-contact.

This is a wheat-forward Japanese noodle shop. The menu is built on udon and soba (wheat noodles), with broths that are soy- and dashi-based and donburi that include tempura. There is no indication of any gluten-free preparation, and shared pots, broth, and prep surfaces make cross-contamination essentially unavoidable. Treat as not celiac-safe.
Broths and donburi sauces rely on standard Japanese soy sauce and dashi, which typically contain wheat. No wheat-free soy alternative is indicated.

No vegan or vegetarian-specific options are documented. Dashi broths are fish/bonito-based and many dishes include meat, egg, or fishcake, so even noodle dishes are not vegan. Shared broth and prep make vegan cross-contact likely.

This is an udon and shokudo kitchen built around wheat. Udon noodles, Chinese noodles (chuka soba), tonkatsu, and karaage all contain wheat, and they share the same kitchen, water, and surfaces. There is no indication of any gluten-free preparation, so it is not suitable for celiacs or anyone needing strict gluten avoidance.
Set meals, donburi, and noodle broths are built on a Japanese dashi and soy-sauce base. Standard Japanese soy sauce is brewed with wheat, so these dishes should be treated as containing wheat/gluten.

Dishes rely on fish-based dashi, egg, chicken, pork, and fish cake (kamaboko), and signature items like keiran udon, oyakodon, and the chicken hot-pot set are animal-based. There are no documented vegan options, and broths and shared cooking surfaces make animal-free dining impractical here.

Not celiac-safe. The food here is oden simmered in a shared dashi/soy-based broth. Many oden tane (fishcakes, hanpen, fried items) contain wheat and soy, and the single simmering pot shares ingredients across the whole menu, so assume cross-contamination throughout. No gluten-free accommodation is indicated.
The oden broth is dashi/soy-based. Most Japanese soy sauce is brewed with wheat, so the broth itself should be treated as containing gluten.

Not suitable for vegans. Oden broth is built on dashi (typically bonito and/or kombu) and the same pot simmers fish, fishcakes, eggs and meat items like beef tendon, so plant-based items would share the animal-based broth.

This is a tonkatsu specialist: pork is breaded in wheat flour and panko and deep-fried, and the menu also features croquettes, shrimp fries, and cream croquettes. With a single owner running one fryer for all of these breaded items, shared-fryer cross-contamination with wheat is effectively unavoidable. Not celiac-safe.

The house signature is a grated-daikon/onion sauce built on a demi-glace and Worcester-style base, which is typically wheat- and soy-derived. Set meals also include a pork soup (tonjiru) made with dashi and miso. These add further gluten exposure beyond the breading.

The Worcester/demi-glace-style sauce and the miso/dashi pork soup are soy- and wheat-derived; most Japanese soy sauce and Worcester sauce contain wheat. Assume gluten is present in the sauces and soup.

This is a pork-focused shop. Even the vegetable sides arrive within sets built around fried pork, and the signature pork soup is meat-based, so there is no realistically vegan meal here and cross-contact with animal products is pervasive.
